newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: SWISSAIR LOSS NARROWS, SEES PROFITS.
newsitem.headline: SWISSAIR LOSS NARROWS, SEES PROFITS.

text.p: The Swissair Group on Friday reported a narrower loss in the first half of 1996 and predicted a return to profitability for the full year.

Describing 1996 as a year of transition, Swissair's chief financial officer Georges Schorderet said airline traffic had not been as strong as expected, but the carrier would still be in the black by the end of the year.
"We will report a positive result for the full year, but our expectations will be reduced slightly based on today's view," Schorderet told Reuters in a telephone interview.

Swissair's first half loss narrowed to 51 million Swiss francs ($42.51 million) from a 86 million franc deficit last year, helped by an improved performance by most of its units, including the core airline and catering operations.
In 1995 Swissair reported a loss of 147 million francs, mainly due to restructuring charges of 340 million francs.
Swissair's first half group revenue rose 10.7 percent to 3.6 billion francs, boosted by recent acquisitions of duty-free business in Australia.
The duty-free activities of Britain's Allders Plc, which Swissair recently acquired, was not included in the results.
First half losses at Swissair are quite normal with the company earning the bulk of its money during the heavy business travel months of September and October.
"Swissair's results really are not that bad," said analyst Roland Leutenegger of Union Bank of Switzerland.
The result was also largely in line with markets' expectations, but Swissair's shares ended the day largely unchanged after initial gains on the result.
"The size of the loss was a positive surprise, we had expected a higher loss. But the forecast is also good," a Swiss share dealer said.
Belgian flagship carrier Sabena, 49.5 percent owned by Swissair, also helped drag the group into the red.
A large part of 27 million franc in losses at associated companies was due to losses at Sabena, which is suffering from the effects of strikes in February.
While the group's catering, hotel and retail activities reported higher earnings, Swissair's core flight operations remain in the red.
"We had higher expectations for traffic figures," said Schorderet, adding that a one percent swing in seat load factor has a 40 million franc impact on the bottom line.

Under the new tough leadership of chief operating officer Philippe Bruggisser, Swissair has embarked on a series of cost-cutting measures to improve flight operations, but these will first start to have a serious effect next year.
"You should not forget that Swissair is a practically a construction site," Schorderet said, noting that .
The measures include a complete overhaul of work processes, concentration of long-haul flights in Zurich, shifting work load abroad and reducing staff.
The aim is to improve the group's bottom line by 500 million francs by 1998, including 100 million in personnel cost that also will be achieved by reducing jobs.
"Some of the action taken to enhance bottom-line performance generates extra costs in the introductory stages, while the benefits may take longer to impact," Swissair said.
Schorderet said Swissair would also be reviewing its entire purchasing activities to try to save costs. However, the company would still not reduce the quality of the Swissair product.
"But must we always buy the most expensive?" asked Schorderet.
($1=1.1995 Swiss Franc)
